# drops

A cross-project issue tracker for AI coding agents. Go, pure-Go SQLite, and
Cobra; one database for every repository, with the project resolved from the
working directory.

**Read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) before working here.** It carries the gate, the
scratch-store rule, the test discipline every ticket is held to, and the tools in
this environment that report success while failing.

Issues live in **GitHub Issues** on
[`tedkulp/drops`](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops), driven by the `gh` CLI —
not in the `drops` store this repo builds. `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` is the
contract for working them; the open queue there is the work queue, and
checked-in notes are not a parallel plan.

The `dw32p` rewrite map that carried this repo to 0.2.0 is closed. Its 79 issues
stay in `~/.drops/drops.db`, which is why `dw32p.N` ids appear in `CHANGELOG.md`
and `docs/research/`.

43	The gofmt check formats what **git** counts as part of this tree — tracked files

72	Four tools lie about success here:
73	
74	- `gofmt -l` exits zero while listing files. The file list is the signal, never `$?`.
75	- `grep -c` exits one on zero matches and silently skips the rest of an `&&` chain.
76	- `go test` prints `ok` for a package whose tests all skipped. Read the skip count
77	  and the test events before treating that output as proof.
78	- `go run` exits 1 whatever its program exited, printing `exit status 3` to stderr.
79	  A recipe that needs the program's own exit code must `go build` and run the binary.

81	## Test discipline
82	
83	The dominant defect in this codebase is a test that appears to cover a requirement
84	but **cannot fail for it**. Coverage does not detect it: `render` and `resolve` sit
85	at 100% function coverage and mutation still found defects in both. Annotated
86	red-checks found zero holes across the reference build; unannotated mutation found
87	every one.
88	
89	So the standard is not a number. It is that each requirement has a **control** — the
90	production branch that makes it true — and that control has been mutated with the
91	test observed **red**.
92	
93	### Which controls get mutated
94	
95	One per **requirement clause**: a behavioural claim the ticket's question names. Not
96	one per test function — that turns the count into the goal and selects for cheap
97	mutations.
98	
99	Where a clause is too coarse to mutate in one place, split it by **load-bearing
100	branch**: parsers, orderings, comparisons, conflict resolution, guards, refusals.
101	Those are where a wrong implementation still passes. A struct that round-trips does
102	not need a control; a comparator does.
103	
104	### How a mutation is run
105	
106	`just mutate`. The four steps are the recipe's, not yours:
107	
108	1. Snapshot the file and record its checksum.
109	2. Apply the mutation.
110	3. Run the one named test, expecting failure. A pass is the finding: the test does
111	   not cover the clause — fix the test, not the record.
112	4. Restore from the snapshot and verify the checksum matches.
113	
114	The snapshot is harness-owned, so **you no longer have to commit first**. `git
115	checkout` was never the restore here — a restore command cannot distinguish a
116	mutation from uncommitted work — and the harness never runs one. A run killed
117	between steps 2 and 4 leaves a journal naming exactly what to put back; the next
118	run refuses to start, and `just mutate --restore` finishes it.
119	
120	Controls live beside the code they mutate, in each package's `mutations.json`: a
121	name, the requirement clause it proves, the file, the `old` → `new` edit, and the
122	test. `just mutate` runs every one; `just mutate core` scopes to a package or a
123	single control name; `--list` prints what is catalogued without running it; and
124	`--file/--old/--new/--test/--clause` runs one ad hoc, for while you are still
125	finding out whether a test can fail at all.
126	
127	It refuses more than it accepts, and every refusal is a finding, never a pass:
128	
129	| It says | It means |
130	|---|---|
131	| `GREEN` | the test passed with the branch broken, so it does not cover the clause |
132	| `NOT RUN` | no test of that name ran — `go test -run` matching nothing prints `ok` and exits 0 |
133	| `BUILD FAILED` | the mutation does not compile, so it proves nothing about the test |
134	| `NO MATCH` | `old` is absent or appears twice; a mutation must name exactly one branch |
135	| `BASELINE RED` | the test was already failing, so its red says nothing |
136	
137	Exit 0 means every control went red, 1 that there is a finding, 2 that it was
138	called wrong, and **3 that a restore failed and the tree may still hold a
139	mutation**.
140	
141	`just mutate` is deliberately not part of `test-all`. The gate asks whether this
142	commit is green; mutation asks whether the suite can fail, and pays a compile per
143	control to answer. Run it when a ticket adds or changes a control.
144	
145	### What a ticket records
146	
147	Enumerate, in `close --reason`: each control (file and behaviour), the test that went
148	red, and confirmation of the restore. `just mutate <package>` prints exactly that, so
149	the enumeration is a by-product rather than prose written from memory, and `--json` is
150	the same record for a machine. A bare count is unauditable — it is the form that let a
151	ticket record "one control" without anyone reading it as "one".
152	
153	A control that is not in a `mutations.json` was proved once and can never be proved
154	again. Catalogue it.
155	
156	### Seams
157	
158	**Discovered facts become constructor parameters; real subsystems stay real.**
159	
160	A fact a process learns about its environment — the writer, terminal-ness, measured
161	width, the pager, the clock, the ID source — is a struct field passed in, never
162	discovered at the point of use. `render` accepts all four of its environment facts,
163	so its whole suite is byte-exact literals with no fake anywhere; the reference build
164	discovered them and needed two package-level variables to make the same behaviour
165	reachable.
166	
167	The datastore is not such a fact. There is deliberately no `Store` interface: every
168	test runs against real temp SQLite, real git, and real `flock`. `synctest` cannot
169	fake SQLite's busy-handler sleep, so lock-contention tests are real-clock. Making
170	these fakeable would trade a real defect class for a faster suite.
171	
172	### Serialized contracts
173	
174	For at least one case per serialized contract, run the real writer and decode its
175	bytes. Deriving both sides from the same description tests the description.
176	
177	### The CLI is a contract
178	
179	`docs/cli-contract.md` is what agents read to drive drops. A verb that
180	changes shape without that file changing is a defect.
181	
182	Every command in the tree carries at least one boundary test through
183	`RunForTest(args, db, cwd)`, asserting what the doc says a reader observes: a
184	byte-exact row for a scanning verb, the JSON shape for a reading verb, the store
185	effect for a mutating verb. A census test walks the command tree and fails on any
186	command absent from the tested-verb registry, so skipping one is an edit to a visible
187	list rather than an omission.

I found one breach of a documented standard: requirement clauses the new tests cover that have no control in `mutations.json`. The rest are judgement-call smells. The changelog, contract, clock seam and scoping of the core controls all follow the repo's rules.

## Documented-standard violations

**Missing controls (hard).** AGENTS.md, "Which controls get mutated", asks for one control per requirement clause, split by load-bearing branch ("comparisons … guards"). It also says: "A control that is not in a `mutations.json` was proved once and can never be proved again. Catalogue it." None of these clauses has an entry in `internal/tui/mutations.json`:
- **Age buckets** (`board.go` `age`): `docs/cli-contract.md` promises exact cut-offs, `m` under an hour, `h` under two days, `d` under sixty days, `mo` under a year, then `y`. None of those comparisons has a control. `TestACardIsThreeLinesByteForByte` only hits `3h`, `5d` and `20m`, so the `mo` and `y` branches and the 48h edge are untested.
- **Age fallback** (`since`): no control on `if moment == nil { return card.created }`.
- **`B` reads nothing** (`toggleBoard`): the `target == m.detailID` → `display` guard has no control, though `TestBReadsNothing…` exists.
- **Tab clears the follow trail** (`switchColumn`): no control on `m.clearFollow()`.
- **Board width** (`measureBoard`): no control on `max(width*2/5, 38)`, the 40% and 38-column rule in the contract.

- **Duplicated Code:** the rule that skips closed issues in `m.all` appears twice (`boardCards`: `if card.status == model.StatusClosed { continue }`, and `boardLoaded`). If one changes, the footer count and the board drift apart. `firstColumn(m.first, int(m.focus), shownColumns(...))` is worked out three times (`pageBoard`, `boardBody`, `boardTitle`).

- **Mysterious Name:**
  - `card` is both a function (`card(candidate row, …)`) and a common `row` parameter name (`columnOf(card row)`, `since(card row, …)`).
  - The Model field `first int` gives no hint that it is the leftmost column on screen.

  - `w` in `boardBody` is cryptic.
- **Primitive Obsession:**

  - `selected := -1` stands for "this column isn't focused" in `columnBody`.
  - `step := 1` / `-1` stands for the tab direction.

- **Middle Man:** `core.ClosedIssues` only passes the call to the store. The neighbouring core reads (`Issues`, `Issue`) do the same, though, so the repo's own convention wins here.
